stem.text: Determine whether the series \( \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n \), where \( a_n = \frac{4}{n^{\frac{2}{3}}} \), converges or diverges. Name a test whose conditions the series meets and state the verdict it gives.

answer_key.label: The series diverges by the p-series test, because \( p = \frac{2}{3} \le 1 \).

worked_solution.text: The general term is \( \frac{4}{n^{\frac{2}{3}}} \), a constant multiple of \( \frac{1}{n^{\frac{2}{3}}} \), so the p-series test fits: the terms are positive and the series is a p-series times \( 4 \).
worked_solution.rule_named: match the form to a test

worked_solution.text: Here \( p = \frac{2}{3} \), and a p-series converges exactly when p is greater than 1.
The series diverges by the p-series test, because \( p = \frac{2}{3} \le 1 \).

options.label: The series converges by the alternating series test, because \( a_n \) decreases to 0.
options.derivation: the alternating series test named for a series of positive terms, its alternating hypothesis never checked

options.label: The series converges by the p-series test, because \( p = \frac{2}{3} < 1 \).
options.derivation: the p-series threshold reversed, so p less than 1 read as convergence

options.label: The series diverges by the p-series test, because \( p = \frac{2}{3} \le 1 \).
The series converges by the nth term test, because \( \lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = 0 \).
options.derivation: convergence concluded from the terms approaching 0, a condition that is necessary but never sufficient
